cells.tense: A choice of connection is being made and you are in it now.
cells.act: defend the direction you chose against the next push
cells.ask: Name the direction you already chose, quietly to yourself. When the next push comes to bend it, hold the line once. One hold, then check whether the choice still fits.
cells.core:
You're where a connection stops being a maybe and becomes a yes, and you can feel which way it's moving. The whole road doesn't need to be clear for that. Enough light for the next step is what you work with. So you choose, and two streams move as one for a while.

When the meeting is doing the work, the heading comes out of it, not out of a plan made alone: you feel someone's direction and move with it. Keep your hand on the heading you picked. When a pull comes to bend you away, don't argue it down. Stay with it once and notice whether the choice holds. Give the person close to you the same steadiness you're giving your own feet.
cells.sheetLine: Feeling sets the direction and you hold it.
cells.verb: meeting a stream of feeling and choosing to flow with it
cells.place: where you move through not knowing without forcing the road clear

cells.tense: You will be braced for a pull that has not found you yet.
cells.act: rest in the result of the tending
cells.ask: Sit with something your care already grew — a friendship, a stretch of work, a slow skill — for a week, adding nothing. Let it be done enough, and notice what leaving it alone is like.
cells.core:
A connection is being pushed toward a togetherness it hasn't reached, and the pushing is happening in advance. The pull is watched for before it arrives, so the meeting gets crowded before anything has met. Wanting the flow to stay turns into standing over it. The idea runs past the experience that would fill it.

The merging happens because enough has been lived first, and then there's something to move with. It doesn't need forcing from above. So take something your care already grew and sit in it this week without adding to it. Let the person near you keep their own footing, and leave the space around them open. That space isn't a gap. It's where the meeting was going to happen.

cells.tense: You were at that door and you are still standing there.
cells.act: distinguish what is yours from what you borrowed
cells.ask: Take five pulls you feel right now and write each one down. Beside each, mark whether it started with you or came in from elsewhere. Don't act on the page. Just read it back.
cells.core:
A meeting that wanted to happen a while back didn't get decided, and the not-deciding is where you stay. The connections around you hold at one-way or go unmade, and you read the room without joining it, waiting for the pull to declare itself. The step past not-knowing didn't get taken, and the hours between you and the other person keep adding up.

You carry many strands and know which are actually yours, and the mixing happens. Seeing doesn't need the whole road. It just has to land. So put the pulls on paper and mark which you brought along. You don't have to act on any of them, and nothing you picked up is wrong. Knowing where one pull ends is enough to feel the next tug.

cells.tense: A path is being shown by you and credited to no one at all.
cells.act: show someone the way you found
cells.ask: Think of something you worked out the hard way. Hand someone the route — the turns, not the story — plainly, once. Then let them walk it without you behind them.
cells.core:
Those near you find their way because you know where the road turns, and if asked to account for it you'd say you happened to be standing there. A direction is being lived, by others and by you, and the one who knows the way won't sign for it.

The directions come from a practice that isn't forced, and being alone with it connects you instead of shutting you in. So take something you worked out the hard way and hand over the turns to someone who needs them — once, plainly. Then let them walk it alone. Your way of knowing is a route someone can follow, not a mood in the air, and it can carry your name at the bottom of the page.
